utterances.text: There you go. Keep going and take a moment to look through those photographs, please. Could we move one or two pages ahead on the e-court, please? Mr. Lazarevic, I'm not going to ask you any questions about the text on the first page or two of this document. I'm interested in the photographs that come later. Thank you. If we could actually move one page further in e-court, I would be grateful. Thank you. And Mr. Lazarevic, what is depicted in these photographs that you have before you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These photographs show fragments of the bombs belonging to the Orkan rocket system. These were surface-to-surface rockets. Each rocket contained 285 bomblets, which were the ones that exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you a specific question. Do you know if the pieces of rocket and the bomblets that are shown in these photographs, were they recovered from Zagreb and the surrounding area? Do you know if that's right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything we can see here on the photographs are fragments or parts of the rockets which directly concern this particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we're at the time for the break, and that completes my questions about this document. I'm very near the end of my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a short break and come back at a quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you've been patient with my questions, and I appreciate that. I just have a couple more for you. First, and we're done with the documents, so you can put those aside. Thank you. My next question is the following: What was the atmosphere among the civilian population of Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995 and in the subsequent days?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, during these critical days of the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995, in my assessment there was general chaos, people were puzzled, and wondered what was going to come next. There was extensive media coverage of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the topic of media coverage, during these days in May 1995, which you've described, did you ever see the accused, Milan Martic, appear in the media?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him appear on television. I can't tell you exactly the date. It may have been the 2nd or the 3rd. I can't tell you because I was quite busy on those days. But I do recall seeing him. I recall this one clip where Mr. Martic gave a statement about all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you describe a little bit more, maybe what he said and what you saw in that video?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall a rather short clip. I can't tell you precisely how long it was, perhaps a minute or a bit more. I remember seeing him on television surrounded by several persons in camouflage uniform, when Mr. Martic said, and now I can't quote his exact words, but I recall him roughly saying that he had ordered the attack and, if I remember well, that more was to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to show you trial Exhibit 388, which is a short video clip. And for this again we'll use the Sanction, please. So if we could switch to the Sanction system, from e-court. And Your Honours, once we switch to Sanction, I think it will still be on the e-court button, if I remember from yesterday. There we go. And if we could begin the clip now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Dear brothers and sisters, your eminence. I wish to address you with a few words and tell you about the situation that has befallen us and about what we plan to do next in order to get out of all this. First of all, I want to tell you that I sincerely sympathise with all the suffering that you have endured. I would have preferred the situation to be good and that I'd come to attend a wedding in Western Slavonia instead of having to come here when you're in your darkest hour to explain how to get out of it and how to find a way out of all this, so that you don't wander around and in order that we may keep our land. We had a meeting here with civilian authorities, the military leadership, and our archpriests. What Croatia has done to us is undoubtedly a crime which was supported by foreign powers; America and Germany. This was not a treason. This was solely the case that our enemy had the upper hand at that point and managed to take control of the motorway and of this part, as you yourselves know. But I'm telling you, one battle doesn't mean that the war has been lost. As a counter-measure to what Tudjman did to you here, we have shelled all their cities, Sisak several times, and Karlovac, and Zagreb yesterday and today. This was done for your sake. But let me tell you that the attack by Tudjman's forces did not focus only on Western Slavonia. They also attacked Lika and Dalmatia. Lika managed to defend itself, and in Dalmatia their forces were removed from Mount Dinara. Today, an ultimatum follows. If they continued to attack our besieged forces, we will continue to attack Zagreb and destroy their cities. Then they begged us to stop shelling Zagreb and said that they let our people out of the encirclement, which is what interests you most."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, did you recognise this video we just watched?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that the statement by Milan Martic that you had just described earlier?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the statement that was frequently broadcast on almost all television stations and over the radio, even several times during one day, whenever there was a news report on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lazarevic, good afternoon. My name is Predrag Milovancevic. I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Martic. We are about to start cross-examining you, and I will be putting questions to you which are relevant for the Defence, and these questions will, as a rule, concern your own profession, you being a police officer, and based on your CV we can say that you are a very experienced police officer. I kindly ask you to make a small pause before answering my questions, so that we could facilitate the work of the interpretation service. I am sure that both you and I will bear this in mind and try not to speed. Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic, from what I can see concerning your personal background in the statement provided by the OTP, you spent your entire career on the police force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Occupying the post of the head of on-site investigations department, your task was to carry out the on-site investigation on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995; isn't that correct? And at the time you were in your office doing your job?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you explained that the police force never operates on its own on a report that it has to go out into the field, it has to wait for the instruction of the investigating judge. On this matter, I would like to ask you the following: I suppose the procedure applied in this particular event was the one you normally applied?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you received the information of the attack on that day, and you knew you had to go out to conduct an on-site investigation. Which were the steps that you took, tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you what the standard procedure is, and of course you have to bear in mind that the standard procedure was also applied in this case. The standard procedure is as follows: The duty service, or, as we call it, the duty service for the operatives, receives the information about the given event. Next, the information is first forwarded to the investigating judge, who, under Article 152/2 are of the Criminal Code, decides to attend the scene or to have the police officers attend the scene. As soon as the duty service forwards the information to the investigating judge, or rather as soon as the duty service forwarded the information on the 2nd of May, the investigating judge used the possibilities provided to him under the Criminal Procedure Act and decided to defer the on-site investigation to the police. I cannot tell you what the reason for his decision was. I only know that he used the discretionary powers granted him under the law. The information went back -- went back from the investigating judge to the duty service where the magistrating judge informed them that they should carry the on-site investigation themselves. Next, the duty service informed the on-site investigations section that they could now proceed to attend the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now kindly ask the usher to distribute copies of your statement given to the OTP to all those in the courtroom. We have copies enough for the Trial Chamber and for you. I needed to provide you with that statement so that I can refer you to a particular item in it that I would wish you to look at. As far as I understood you, when you went through the usual procedure in such cases, you gathered the policemen who were on duty in the numbers you needed them, and went on to attend the scene, to undertake the measures that you usually do in such cases?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since there were several locations in Zagreb to be attended, including several people, you have explained that you didn't carry out the entire on-site investigation by yourself because it would be a physical impossibility, but rather it was attended by the people under your control, and they reported to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards the events of the 2nd of May of 1995, do you remember whether that was a working day? The 1st of May is a holiday, and as a rule the 1st and 2nd were usually both declared holidays. On occasion, it included the 3rd as well. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember what day of the week that was. I don't remember whether it was a regular working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You tried to explain the type of organisation of your unit and the procedures you undertook at the scene. You said that you've put together a document, which is called the official note on the on-site investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I compiled a report pertaining to the events of the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I am now going back to what was discussed yesterday. I believe that on-site investigation report includes some 800 pages, because it contains all the photographs, physicians' findings and everything that is related to the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise. I don't think I said exactly 800 pages, but around that figure, taking all the documentation in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I didn't mean to challenge the figure. I just wanted to sort of provide a picture of the scope of your work.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony in chief you were shown the on-site investigation report being compiled by the general crime section of the Zagreb police administration. This is Exhibit 799. Could we please have it put on the screen, Exhibit 799. While we're waiting for it to be done, Mr. Lazarevic, I wish to remind you that this is the on-site investigation report of the 2nd of May, 1995 stipulating the authorised people to attend the scene and conduct the investigation, as well as all the experts that were needed, including crime technicians and forensic technicians. There seems to be a problem with the locating of this document. I have said already that it is Exhibit 799. Yes, now we have it. Thank you. It seems my comment was premature. We have it before us now. This is the on-site investigation report, and we saw that document yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the number of those injured and killed was mentioned in this on-site investigation report, as is its official title? Can you remember the figures?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise. I believe there were around 130 people involved. I have described all those I managed to identify, but I can't be precise as to the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I wish to assist you. Could we go to page 70 of the document in the B/C/S? In the English that is page 63. On that page we have the description of the wounds of the wounded. Page 70 in the B/C/S, in its upper right corner, the figures are 520. Does your page have 520 in your upper right corner? And under "serious bodily injuries," we have all those wounded mentioned, and each of them is put in a separate paragraph. Is that correct? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please go to page 85 of this document in the B/C/S. In its upper right corner, it bears the number 535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which page would that be in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to provide you with an answer as soon as possible. As far as I can conclude, it is page 78. We come up to the number 107, paragraph 107. The numbering is the same in the B/C/S and in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, on page 85, the last figure above "minor injuries" is 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether His Honour Mr. Hoepfel has managed to locate the figure. I didn't quote the English page number correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's page 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore on page 85 of the B/C/S and page 75 of the English, the last figure is 107 mentioning a person, and her name, and that is the last person which fell under the category of serious bodily injuries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see on the screen that the last person with serious bodily injuries was at number 107, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After that we have minor injuries, beginning with the number 108 onwards. This concludes on page 92 in the B/C/S with the number 160. I again need to apologise to the bench, since I don't know the exact English page. But if you will follow the numbers, you should come up to 160. Mr. Lazarevic, under the number 160, is that the last person with minor bodily injuries? The person's name is Igor Loncaric, Papa?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to answer. I wish I could have the hard copy before me. But that would probably take some time for me to be provided with it. I can't confirm or deny what you've put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to assist us with this, and I ask for your forgiveness to having put you in this situation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is very difficult without a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To assist you, we began on page 70 in the B/C/S, the original language of the report. Please go to page 70.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am already on page 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, please go back to page 70, since you couldn't actually have the text before you a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please continue. And from number 1 until what number we have people with serious bodily injury?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is the number 107. But for me to be able to ascertain that with any degree of certainty I should go page by page to see whether there is a possible error in numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I've checked the document, the numbering is fine. I'm not trying to trap you in any way. It would be highly irresponsible. Could you now please go from 1 to 107?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reached 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this concludes the category of serious bodily injury. Now, please continue to see how many people there were with minor injuries. At page 92 we see the end of that list, the figure there being 160 of those who suffered minor injuries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The list ends with number 160 on page 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under that we have identities of persons killed, mentioning four people whose names you have mentioned, either today or yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These people are Ana Mutevelic, Damir Dracic, Stjepan Krhanj, and Ivanka Kovac. Those people were killed in the attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards this on-site investigation report pertaining to the 2nd of May, 1995 is concerned, you've explained the work of your police administration and your department carried out to establish facts, and this took you almost a month?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it took a while to put all that down to paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the documentation forwarded by the OTP there is a document, since I've mentioned the figures from this report, and that document is entitled "The summary of established facts concerning the terrorist attacks on Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995." This document bears the number 0207-0824. Could we please have it put on the screen. While we're waiting for the document to be put on the screen, I wanted to explain the reason for putting it to you. I wish to establish what the number of those injured was and what was the type of their injuries. In your testimony in chief, you said that there were some changes made, depending on the assessment or the findings of the physicians as regards the injuries of the people involved, and that is quite understandable. The reason why I invoked this document was that according to the on-site investigation report, the number of people who suffered serious bodily injury was 107. We saw the list conclude with 107. The number of those who sustained minor bodily injury was 50, between 107 and the last figure we saw, and that there were four killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Not 50, 53. If I count correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now reach a conclusion on the final figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This report -- or this document was compiled by the Zagreb police administration. Could we please scroll down the page to be able to see the entire page. The title is "Summary of established facts concerning the terrorist attacks on the city of Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995." Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the heap of documents shown to me, it is difficult for me to say. I would like to see who the author of the document is and who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page of the document. In its upper right corner, it bears the number 825. If we go down the page we can see that people are listed. Those people were involved in the on-site investigation on the 2nd of May, 1995. Could we please go back up the page? That's good, thank you. The first person is yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Branko Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At page 26 of the document in the B/C/S, which bears the number 850 in the upper right corner, we have the total number of persons sustaining injuries on the 2nd of May, where the number of those killed -- could we please have -- zoom in on the text, and could you read it out, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says here that four persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just as in the previous report. So that's consistent, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the number of persons who suffered serious injuries. Here it says that there were 50 of them, whereas in your on-site investigation report there were 107 of them. That's almost half of what is stated here. Can you account for the difference in any way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I still haven't seen who the author of the summary report is and I would like very much to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, at what page of the English version of this report could we find this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the other page, we can see that this is the on-site report of the 2nd of May, 1995, bears the number 0307-3250 in the upper right corner, and it is marked as the second page of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version that I have with me here. Page 2, the ERN number is 0307-3250.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Incidentally, since Mr. Lazarevic asked me who signed the report, well, the person who signed the report is Darko Skender, the chief of the sector.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Darko Skender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to do this to you, but I've gone to page 2 and I've gone to page 3. I don't have this table that I see in the B/C/S that gives numbers of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't even give you that information. I only referred you to page 2 and to the page where Mr. Lazarevic's name is contained. As for page 30 in the English, the last three digits in the upper right-hand corner are 278. At the bottom -- I seem to have gone too far now, that's the 3rd of May. Inadvertently I turned to the page concerning the 3rd of May. Page 3 the English text. Your Honour, what we have on our screens in the B/C/S is page 23 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, in this particular report we have 50 as the figure of those who suffered serious injuries, whereas in your report there were 107 of them. Perhaps some of the persons were subsequently reclassified into minor injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But my question to Mr. Lazarevic was how he was able to account for the difference.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a very demanding task and a time-consuming task to prepare these reports. I suspect this report may have been produced a bit earlier, perhaps on the 3rd and the 4th, before all the information had reached the centre, and that is why it is not complete. It took several days for all the information to arrive, for instance, for the medical reports to arrive from hospitals, for instance, the admission papers. Therefore, I allow for the possibility that this figure here is incorrect and that the figures of those injured and the medical qualifications of injuries arrived subsequently. If you go through the papers, you will see that some of the persons subsequently applied for medical assistance in different health-care centres, and this is something that was reported to the police later on. I can't tell you now what the exact numbers of hospitals are, but there were about 30 health-care centres in the entire area, and that is why perhaps the numbers differ, as it took some 25 to 30 days for the matters to settle in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'm interested in the following: In the situation such as this one, or a similar one, you attended scene and you come across a person. What happens next? For instance, in the case of Ms. Ana, we could see that the site was marked with number 1. I suppose that then after the area is secured, a report is produced. But what happens with the body, where is the body taken?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the forensic examination is completed, that is to say after the operative, the inspector, describes the body, the forensic technician takes photographs of the body or draws a sketch of the body, and then the body is taken to the city morgue. There were many forensic technicians that attended the scene marked with number 1. Of course, the person attending that particular scene wouldn't know with what number the site several blocks away would be marked. The forensic technician is only aware of what is happening on his own site. And that is of course true for all the other sites; they wouldn't know of what the others were doing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not switch my microphone on. I told Mr. Lazarevic that I thanked him for his answer and that I understood. In his answer Mr. Lazarevic told us what the conventional procedure is. Whoever attends the scene has to record every single detail so that nothing is left to doubt. Every photograph has its caption. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's described in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in one other thing. When the body of the person killed leaves the hands of the police and goes to the city morgue, we were able to see, according to several reports, that an autopsy is performed on the body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that an obligatory standard procedure that applies to every single body found?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Criminal Procedure Act, there is the obligation to follow such a procedure wherever there is reasonable suspicion to believe that there was foul play. When the police carries out the on-site investigation, the referral or the application for an autopsy is normally filed by the police -- or, rather, it is normally done by the investigating judge, but where it is not, then it is done by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But is it the standard procedure that the police has to be informed, or rather one has to report to the police every such incident where there is suspicion of a crime?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, where there is reasonable suspicion to doubt that there was a crime committed. But I'm not sure what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the standard procedure. When you come across a dead body, isn't it the standard procedure that this is reported to the police in order for the police to carry out the procedure as you described it now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the standard procedure, but I don't know what your question is aimed at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the number of those injured or killed on the 2nd of May, and I'm speaking now only of the 2nd of May, 1995, we have gone through a number of documents and you explained how this all went. In your statement which is before you, and I mean paragraph 19 of the statement you gave to the OTP, you stated that you reviewed reports of all persons -- rather, that the reports were shown to you by the OTP. Could you please take a look at paragraph 19 of your statement. That's the statement you gave to the OTP on the 14th and 15th of February, 2005. That's page 9, paragraph 19 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the English version. Perhaps there is -- this whole document is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall -- well, I don't recall ever receiving the statement in the B/C/S, but we managed somehow anyway. You go on to explain the following. I was shown the medical reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. I wasn't a hundred per cent clear, but if what's needed is a B/C/S copy of the statement, I do have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, in paragraph 19 of your statement you state that you were shown medical reports of the victims on the 2nd of May. You state that these reports were contained in your on-site investigation report, and then you went on to list the names of the victims. That's under paragraph 19. Have all the documents of all the victims who were injured or killed on the 2nd of May, 1995 shown to you? Why am I asking you this? We have a list of all the victims here, and according to paragraph 19, there was a total of 128 victims, which is again different to what we currently have own screens, 154 were victims. It is also different to the figure alleged in the indictment, where the Prosecutor gave yet another figure. Have you really been shown documents concerning all the victims that are contained in paragraph 19?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2005, when I spoke to the gentlemen, they did show me the documents and I reviewed them. But I can't be sure that I wasn't mistaken with regard to this or other person. In retrospect, given the lapse of time, it is almost impossible for me to answer the question. It would take quite a while for me to sit down and peruse the papers and compare them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've understood what you're saying. Mr. Lazarevic, I put this question to you because in the indictment that was initially filed the Prosecution gives one figure of victims. Then this figure was corrected in the subsequent indictment. They speak of at least five killed and 146 injured. Whereas in paragraph 19 there is the figure which I counted several times, and I might be mistaken in one or two persons but not more than that, the number given is 128. So you can't tell us anything more than what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would take me quite a while to try and take all this in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Nowhere in paragraph 19 of the statement does it purport to give a comprehensive number of the victims who were injured, nor does it suggest that those medical records that are listed here represent all of the victims. So if that's what Mr. Milovancevic is suggesting, then he is misrepresenting -- well, it's not evidence because it's not in evidence, but he's misrepresenting what's in this statement. If not, I'm not clear what the alleged inconsistency is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, much earlier I heard Mr. Milovancevic saying, "Are you sure you've recorded all." But I wasn't quite sure whether he was talking about this paragraph or another paragraph, so I was waiting to hear. Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any answer to that question? Paragraph 19 starts by saying: "I was shown the following medical reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I merely asked the witness whether the Prosecution showed him all the documentation relative to the victims. That was the gist of my question. Because this entire page contains names of victims and numbers of documents. I asked him whether he could assist us in any way. I don't know what the text of this statement means, whether he was presented with only some victims or with all of the victims. But perhaps the witness should read for us what is contained in paragraph 19 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Milovancevic. Wait a minute, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have been saying to this witness, you have counted 128 here, there are a certain number on the indictment. There is a number of 50 on the document that's on the screen, and there is a number of 160 on his report. And you are saying what is the correct number. Now, the witness doesn't need to read paragraph 19 for us. We can read it for ourselves. "I was shown the following medical reports." He's not suggesting that these are all the reports of the victims, he's not suggesting that these are all the reports that he got from the Prosecution. I don't know whether he is able -- you can ask him. I don't know whether he is able to tell you whether the Prosecution showed him all. For him to know that the Prosecution showed him all, he must be able to have seen all. All I'm saying to you is the issue that you are raising is that there are -- there is inconsistency in the numbers, and the objection that has been raised is, the number that is at paragraph 19 does not purport to be an exhaustive list. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor's objection and his explanation for what is stated in number -- in paragraph number 19 is, then I will paraphrase my question, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paraphrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, in this paragraph of your statement, and I'm not trying to entrap you in any way, all I want to know is what were you trying to indicate in this paragraph 19? Was it the documents you saw and what victims are these? Are these all of the victims of the attack on the 2nd of May or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerned all victims in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions on this topic. Let us move on then. In the report for the 3rd of May, 1995, in paragraph 20 you mention that medical reports were shown to you. As regards the 3rd of May, were you also shown medical reports of the victims of that shelling by the OTP and were those all the victims of the attack on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think this is conflating two ideas. The witness has testified that he wrote a report back in May of 1995. Many years later he has an interview with the OTP in which he is shown some documents. But it's unclear to me whether the question asked him if he reviewed the necessary medical reports when he drafted his report back in 1995, or whether he reviewed the medical reports when he gave his statement in 2005. I would object on the basis it is an unclear and for that reason unfair question to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for being imprecise. I wanted to put paragraph 20 to the witness of his own statement. Given the context of that paragraph, I wanted to ask him whether, during his conversation with the OTP back in 2005, was he shown all medical documents pertaining to the victims on the 3rd of May, 1995. Because that's what paragraph 20 is about. This is my interpretation of it. I don't know whether the witness spoke about all victims or just a part of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is the problem, and this is the problem that I raised a little earlier. How can he say whether he's seen all. He says in the statement, "I saw the following, I was shown the following." That's what he saw. He's not saying all, he's not saying some. He is just saying, "What I've written down here is what I was shown on this occasion." Now whether this is all or not all, I don't know. And I don't know whether he will be able to remember that or he can tell you that. The only way he can do it, as he said much earlier, he said to you, "I would need time to go through these papers," and for him to go through these papers, it means he must now go away and count all these, check these names against his own report. And having checked it against his report, only then can he come back and say what the OTP showed me on this statement was either all or not all. If you want that, you can do that, you can take an adjournment and he can go and study his papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. I understand your instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've given no instruction. I have given no instruction. I have just said that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise yet again. I don't mean to say that you've said something you didn't. I withdraw the previous remark. I wanted to ask the witness what the meaning of the sentence in paragraph 20 is, just before the names and figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is the sentence, the last sentence of paragraph 20 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained already the way I compiled the document. I said I used all medical reports when drafting it. That was the basis of my work. That would be the gist of this sentence. Therefore, when I was drafting the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The on-site investigation report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There I used only medical reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the last sentence you said you used the originals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So what is this list that follows? Are those the original documents?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those are not the originals. I copied into the document from the originals I had. But this list is not a complete list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is the list of the originals you included in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we have 36 victims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry, Judge, you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you just said this is not a complete list. And this remark was overheard, probably, by Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I did want to raise with you, Mr. Milovancevic, was that obviously the list that comes underneath there cannot be an original. That's just a list. The sentence says, "I was drafting my final on-site investigation report and the originals are attached to my final report." Not this document. The originals of, I suppose, the medical reports themselves are attached to my final report. I don't know what the originals these are of. But whatever originals they are, they are at the final report, not on this document. I don't know whether that's what you meant to say, sir, but this is how I understand your statement. You can explain yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I understood it as well, Your Honour. But by your leave, I wish to conclude this topic by one final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, could you please read out that sentence. I know you've spent quite a lot of time testifying.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I referred to the same medical records when I was drafting my final on-site investigation report and the originals are attached to my final report."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's what the last sentence reads?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a column at the end of the sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What follows is the list of documents and names of people. I believe this number refers to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That refers to the number of a document, I presume.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of what this list is supposed to represent, the name of all the people in your report or not, or just a few?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of all the people that this sentence refers to, those wounded and mentioned in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that those people were injured on the 3rd of May, 1995 and those people are mentioned in your on-site investigation report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you yet again, in order for me to give you a definitive answer, I would have to go through the entire documentation. For example, Almira Osmanovic, specifically I know that she had been injured. She is a famous ballet dancer, and she was injured on the 3rd of May. But as for the other people, I would have to sit down and go through all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes this topic, Mr. Lazarevic. I thank you for your answer. The rocket attack, or the shelling, or whatever we call it that took place in Zagreb on the 2nd or the 3rd of May, 1995 took place after the 1st of May. What happened on the 1st of May of that year? Do you remember? What began happening on that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember it clearly and correctly, I believe the Croatian Operation Flash began, the police operation. I believe that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you link this attack on Zagreb to that operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't do that. My job was to conduct on-site investigations. It could have happened a month earlier or a month before, for all I care.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The explosions took place on the 2nd of May. Were the citizens advised to pay attention, to be more alert, and was such a warning issued by the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry of Defence, after having heard the reports you've mentioned yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question. There was some general instruction on how people should behave in case of air strikes, but I don't know whether I read your question correctly. No one in Zagreb could have known what would take place on the 2nd of May. Therefore, I presume none of them were hiding or could have been hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What do you think did the Croatian government know what was happening in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to answer that. I can only assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That suffices, thank you. Gojko Susak, the then Minister of Defence, said that there were 400 people of Serb ethnicity killed in Western Slavonia. Do you know whether a single person out of that figure was brought to the forensic institute?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have such information. This figure you've mentioned, the 400, I've never heard of it before, and I don't know who it was that Gojko Susak told it to. I don't think that was in the media; at least I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, a forensic institute where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Zagreb. The forensic institute in Zagreb, whether they had any such data.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At this point I will object, Your Honour, on the grounds of relevance. I don't see what could be the possible relevance of 400 people of Serb ethnicity killed in Western Slavonia to the charges in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have an objection, Mr. Milovancevic. Do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had they been doing their job, it would have been clear to them. But it seems they weren't doing that. On the same day we had five killed in Zagreb and the 400 killed in Western Slavonia. One must be able to establish some sort of a link between the two. There was the clip with Mr. Martic, and there is some relevance to it. He said this was to take revenge because of Tudjman's actions. I believe it to be quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Whether or not Operation Flash was somehow connected to the decision to shell Zagreb is one thing. Now, crimes committed in that is another thing, and how that can -- at this Tribunal we have many cases. And each case deals with alleged criminal responsibility of one person, and that case has to deal with those charges. Now, crimes that may have been committed in other places in the former Yugoslavia are the subject of other cases. Unless Defence counsel can articulate how the alleged death of these 400 people impacts on the charges in this case, our position is that it's irrelevant and the question should not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may reply, Your Honours. The Prosecutor has shown us a clip with Mr. Martic explaining to the population that Croatia committed a crime against the Serbian population in Western Slavonia and that in his view it was supported by some foreign powers, and that because of Tudjman's activities the Serbs counter-attacked, and he said should they continue to attack our besieged forces, we will strike back. I understand that there are other cases before this Tribunal, but I don't think anyone has been charged with the crimes committed during the Flash operation. And Mr. Grujic said that there were 168 bodies found in Western Slavonia. My next question would be to this witness whether those 168 were transferred to the pathology department at the forensic institute, or is it still unknown where those bodies came from and who they were? Therefore, this person before us is an on-site investigation expert, and I'm interested in whether he knows that, or whether 168 corpses were indeed brought to the institute. Therefore, I need to set a background to my following question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me start off by saying the other day when you referred to 168 bodies, this Chamber told you that if you do want to criticise your learned friend, and it happens to be the same learned friend who is conducting the proceedings today, if you wanted to criticise him for having not indicted the people who are responsible for the death of the 168 and you were getting sick, as you did say, of him not doing so, you must do that outside of this court. This is what the Court told you the other day. Now -- I'm not done with you. You have now just clearly said it, that this witness is an on-site inspector, criminal investigator. Now, he is -- his area of jurisdiction was in Zagreb, not in Western Slavonia. He does not work in the -- how do you call that place? What institute did you call that? Forensic institute. He works as a policeman. He deals with criminality that takes place within his area of operation, which was Zagreb. I don't know how you expect this witness to know whether the 168 people went to a forensic institute in Zagreb. And are there no forensic institutes in Slavonia, Western Slavonia? In any case, you are saying that those were Serb people killed -- were you anticipating that the Serb people would be taken to a Croatian hospital, forensic institute in a situation where Serbs were fighting against Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not insist on this question any further, but I just want to give you an explanation. I raise this matter not because I was dissatisfied with the work of my learned friend. I am not in the position to do that. But this Trial Chamber should not render any decisions in this case until one question is raised, which is basic. Would there have been Zagreb had there not been Flash? That is why I put the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that. And that is not the purpose of the indictment. I think if there was -- if there was a Western Slavonia or if there was a Flash, that people who were involved in Flash must be charged. That's -- that's the sense in which I said to you if you have problems with your learned colleague, have them outside this court, because that's a matter for another case. Now, this witness here is testifying on what happened in Zagreb. This Trial Chamber has told you in a decision some time back that revenge is not a defence in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. And I have never heard of it being a defence anywhere else. For the first time today, you have stated it quite categorically that what took place in Zagreb was revenge. This is the first time I've heard you put it as clearly as you did a couple of minutes ago. And, in fact, you also implied to us just by saying had there been no Western Slavonia, would there have been Zagreb. Now, if that's your defence in this case, that may be your defence, but understand that some of the things that you deal with become irrelevant to the indictment in this case, because revenge is not a defence in this case. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have one more question to put to the witness. I will not insist on the questions I have been putting so far. But in response to what you said, I must tell you that this was not the revenge at -- as an issue now. The fact that the Trial Chamber mentioned revenge before the Defence case would be premature. Only after the Trial Chamber has heard the evidence led by the Prosecution and the evidence by the Defence can it decide about what happened in Zagreb. But to mention it at this stage is premature. I have only one more question for the witness, and if you agree, I would like to put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could he show us on this map the location of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb? Was this between the Proletarski Brigada and Savska Streets? Isn't it a large building there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit 804 on our screens, that's the map we've been using. This would complete our cross-examination and would be helpful both for the Trial Chamber and all those present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Black, are you able to see the map? Would you like to come this side?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think I will be able to see on the video screen. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 804, please. That's one portion of this map. It's the top left-hand corner marked with this number. I suppose it's right, I hope it's right, because it's the zoomed-in left -- upper left part of the map we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If there are difficulties in locating it, could you please use this map?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. The problem lies in the fact that the street names are not entered here, and it takes me some time to locate them. This is the Savska Street. The Ministry of the Interior should be somewhere here. I've only just found it only to lose it again. In my opinion, it should be somewhere below this marking here. This is the Savska Street.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milovancevic. Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what the building is like. Are there several buildings there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll describe it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, we have it on our screens now. Could we please zoom in on the upper left corner? I thank the usher for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, it should be somewhere below the marking number 5. It's the intersection of the Savska Street and the Vukovar Avenue. It's a three-storey building, some 150 by 80 metres in footprint, and it's at the crossing of Savska and what used to be Proletarski Brigada Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether MUP members took part in Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer to that question because I myself did not participate in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you can't, Mr. Lazarevic, that's very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. I have completed my cross-examination. I tried to finish my cross-examination today in view of our tomorrow's situation with the videolink. Thank you. And I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, for your patience and your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, no questions, just one clarification, if I could. Just for the record to state when the witness pointed to the map and said -- in reference to number 5, he said that it should be underneath the yellow box to number 5, and I don't see that that is clear in the transcript, and I just wanted it for accuracy to be reflected in the record, if the Defence has no objection. I think that's a correct characterisation of what he indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Lazarevic? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said where the MUP building was located, at the intersection of Savska Cesta and Vukovar Avenue. On this map, it should be below the rectangular marking containing the explosion sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Obviously, I don't know whether the other Judges have questions for this witness. Okay. Judge Hoepfel has one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, may I just, for clarification, summarise from your official reports on the 2nd and on the 3rd of May. The list of killed persons identified in these reports, if I understand you correctly, they don't contain all persons who died from these incidents but only four persons who were immediately killed on the 20th -- on the 2nd of May and one person killed on the 3rd of May. This is Ivan Markulin. And in addition, there were one person who died in consequence of the attacks on the 2nd of May, and this was Ivan Brodar, and one person as a result of the 3rd of May, who was Luka Skracic. Is that correct? Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You've listed them correctly. In the report concerning the 2nd of May, only those persons are mentioned who got killed on the spot and whom we found at the sites of impact. Mrs. Ivanka Kovac died shortly after reaching the hospital. These were the four persons I entered in my on-site investigation report because I was sure of their death. The next day I only mentioned the police officer Ivan Markulin who I knew died instantaneously on that day. Several days later, after having been treated, Ivan Brodar and Luka Skracic died in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from Judge Hoepfel's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lazarevic, thank you very much for coming to testify. We appreciate your time and effort. And this brings us to the end of your testimony. You are now excused, you may stand down. Thank you very much once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned to tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.00, same court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24
